A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MLMP research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original segmentation experiments, component ablations, computational measurements, and qualitative results.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, alongside new ACDC and GTA-V evaluations and experiments on prompt length, adaptation iterations, and online adaptation.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same LayerNorm adaptation, intermediate-layer fusion, entropy-based inference weights, global CLS loss, and multi-prompt objective. The added experiments vary backbones and adaptation protocols without revising the proposed MLMP components.

E1.justification: v2 adds ACDC driving scenes under real fog, night, rain, and snow, including reference images, and GTA-V rendered urban scenes. These extend the retained datasets and synthetic corruptions to explicitly adverse real conditions and rendered imagery; the reported benchmark expands from seven datasets and 82 scenarios to nine and 87.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods, including TENT, TPT, WATT, and CLIPArTT in v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5. New experiments use existing non-adapted and TENT controls. Long-CLIP serves as an experimental backbone, rather than a newly competing adaptation method.

E3.justification: v2 adds one-step adaptation, online updates carrying parameters between batches, and Long-CLIP experiments with three textual-input variants. ACDC reference and adverse views are adapted independently. These introduce substantive experimental protocols; the original ten-step, batch-size-two episodic settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices H-J and Tables 14-16 examine prompt verbosity, dependence on adaptation iterations, and episodic versus online adaptation. They test previously unexamined sensitivity and error-accumulation questions. Existing component, layer, template-count, backbone, and qualitative failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The Figure 1 caption newly specifies that its variance is computed across all samples and corruptions, clarifying uncertainty reporting. Both versions otherwise specify three repetitions with means and standard deviations; no increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Retained tables have unchanged numerical results. New Table 6 reports ACDC adverse-condition averages of 30.28 for MLMP, 26.29 for TENT, and 23.35 without adaptation; GTA-V scores are 28.84, 26.62, and 25.09 respectively. Tables 14-16 add prompt and protocol findings, including online V20-C performance of 71.77 versus 77.58 episodically. These are additional conditions, not revised same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Equations 1-11, Proposition 1, and its Appendix A proof retain the same mathematics. The variance bound and the independence assumption used in the proof are unchanged; no new theorem or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the benchmark contribution to nine datasets and 87 scenarios, explicitly including real and rendered shifts. The central novelty, plug-and-play applicability, and multi-level/multi-prompt adaptation claims retain their previous meaning.

C2.justification: Appendix J adds an important applicability limitation: online adaptation underperforms episodic adaptation. It proposes error accumulation and model drift as explanations and discusses possible remedies. v2 also interprets longer-prompt behavior and qualifies ACDC reference comparisons because scene contents can differ. The original shared-projection-head limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents ACDC processing with 224-by-224 patches and 112-pixel overlap, and describes ChatGPT-generated extended prompts with examples. Core implementation details remain unchanged. The repository target is identical, although v2 explicitly states that both code and data are available.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Table 1 add a localized comparison with domain generalization, few-shot segmentation, and test-time training. Additional references cover these paradigms, the new datasets, Long-CLIP, TULIP, and adaptation pitfalls. The original positioning as the first fully test-time adaptation framework for OVSS is retained.

P1.justification: There are localized language and cross-reference edits, shorter titles for Sections 3 and 4, and added correspondence information. Three appendix sections are inserted, moving former Appendices H-J to K-M. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the presentation: the paradigm comparison, ACDC/GTA-V results, three prompt/protocol analyses, and detailed ACDC reference/adverse results. Existing figures and tables are retained and reflowed, with Figure 1 receiving caption clarification. The substantial change is the new comparative displays, not pagination alone.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central robustness claim through direct adverse-weather and rendered-domain evaluations beyond v1's synthetic corruptions and standard datasets. The new budget and online studies also expose practical behavior, especially dependence on resets, addressing important validation and applicability gaps. Table 14's optimistic interpretation of longer text deserves qualification because extended class descriptions lower absolute accuracy, but this limited weakness does not outweigh the stronger evidence and clearer limitations.
